ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: An extracellular esterase (HP) with polybutylene succinate (PBS)-degrading ability was identified from Pseudomonas mendocina SA-1503. The HP also had the ability to degrade poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate) and polycaprolactone. This HP had optimal activity at pH 9.0 and 40 °C and remained stable at pH 8.0–9.0 and temperatures of 30–40 °C. Mn2+ promoted the enzyme activity. HP could hydrolyze all p-NP fatty acid ester substrates containing even numbers of carbon atoms from C2 to C18 and had the highest catalytic activity for the p-NP C6 substrate. After 60 h of HP-catalyzed degradation, PBS films experienced a weight loss of more than 60%. Butanedioic acid, 1,4-butanediol, and a series of oligomers were detected in the degradation products of PBS by HP. Further structural analysis of HP revealed that it could be classified as a microbial esterase of α/β hydrolase superfamily and contained a conserved catalytic triad structure (Ser-148, Asp-198, and His-228) with a relatively exposed active site.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Introduction
ce:section.ce:para: With the increase in plastic use worldwide, the accumulation of plastic waste generated is causing serious environmental pollution (Shimao, 2001). There has been an increase in global production of plastics from 2 million tons in 1950 to 450 million tons in 2019 (Bahl et al., 2021). It is expected to reach 500 million tons by 2025, approximately 60% of which will turn into plastic waste in the environment (Zhang et al., 2021). Most of the plastics are produced from petroleum resources and are not environmentally degradable. This implies that the accumulation of these plastic wastes in the environment will continue to harm the ecosystems (Chae and An, 2018; Swapan Kumar, 2013; Willis et al., 2018).

One approach to address the above problem is to develop and commercialize biodegradable plastics (BPs), such as polybutylene succinate (PBS), polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT), and polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) (Abou-Zeid et al., 2001; Barletta et al., 2022; Jost, 2018; Urbanek et al., 2022). Among these plastics, PBS is an aliphatic polyester synthesized by the polycondensation of succinic acid and 1,4 butanediol widely used in the fields of agriculture (Liu et al., 2024), food packaging (Chuayjuljit et al., 2017; Vytejčková et al., 2017), and biomedical materials (Aliotta et al., 2022; Liminana et al., 2018; Rafiqah et al., 2021), due to its good mechanical properties.

The degradation of BPs occurs by enzymes produced by some microorganisms in the environment. This degradation process is mainly divided into two steps. In the first step, microorganisms bind to the surface of BPs and then colonize and form biofilms (Gu, 2003). After that, degrading enzymes are produced to hydrolyze long polymer chains into short-chain oligomers or monomers. In the second step, the decomposed oligomers and monomers are absorbed and utilized by microorganisms and mineralized into harmless small molecules such as CO2 and H2O (Brannigan and Dove, 2016; Luckachan and Pillai, 2011; Pathak and Navneet, 2017). In recent years, researchers have isolated some PBS depolymerase from the environment. Serine protease (1200 U/mL) isolated from Laceyella sacchari LP175 can degrade PBS (100 g/L) by up to 46.5 ± 2.05% at 50 °C in 48 h (Samaimai et al., 2021). An esterase, JY35_02679, produced by Bacillus sp. JY35 exhibited PBS degradation activity. The incubation of PBS films with recombinant E. coli containing the JY35_02679 gene for 10 d in liquid culture at 30 °C leads to about 45.7% weight loss of the films (Kim et al., 2023). Lipase from Pseudomonas cepaci can efficiently degrade PBS and poly(butylene succinate-co-L-lactate) at 50 °C and pH 6.0. The enzymatic degradation of these polymers depends not only on their crystallinities but also on their molecular orientation (Taniguchi et al., 2002). Both cutinase from Fusarium sp. and lipase from Candida antarctica (Lipozyme CALB) showed PBS degradation ability. The weight loss of PBS degraded by cutinase was higher than that degraded by Lipozyme CALB under the same conditions. The mechanism of PBS degradation by cutinase and Lipozyme CALB involves surface erosion and bulk erosion, respectively (Shi et al., 2019).

In this study, potential PBS-degrading enzyme genes in Pseudomonas mendocina SA-1503 (a PBS-degrading strain) were identified using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The expression of these genes was determined, and the PBS degradation ability of the corresponding enzymes was investigated. In addition, the molecular structure of the PBS-degrading enzyme and its mode of interaction with substrates were preliminarily analyzed. This work not only contributes to the understanding of the PBS biodegradation mechanism but also can be applied to the development of more efficient PBS degradation technologies.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Materials and methods
Strain, materials, and culture medium
ce:section.ce:para: More than 50 soil samples were collected from a domestic waste landfill in Fushun, China. One gram of soil sample was added to a PBS-emulsified medium and shaken at 30 °C (150 rpm) for 10 days. The culture was then aspirated and added to the PBS medium under the same conditions for another 10 days. The bacterial solution was diluted and spread on PBS-emulsified plates and incubated at 30 °C. Colonies that formed clear zones were selected and subjected to 16S rDNA gene sequencing. Pseudomonas mendocina SA-1503, which could form a maximum clear zone on PBS medium, was selected for subsequent studies.

PBS (Xinjiang Blue Ridge Tunhe, TH-803S, M w = 9.8 × 104) was used as the testing substrate. Polylactic acid (NatureWorks, 2003D, M w = 12.9 × 104), PCL (Perstorp 6300, M w = 3.3 × 104), PBAT (Xinjiang Blue Ridge Tunhe TH801T, M w = 9.3 × 104), and poly 3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate (P34HB, Tianjin GreenBio, 24 mol% 4HB, M w = 19.5 × 104) were used for the analysis of substrate specificity. PBS films (0.3 mm thickness) were prepared by hot-press method (Wang et al., 2023a). The p-nitrophenyl phosphate (p-NP) fatty acid ester substrates containing an even number of carbon atoms (C2-C18) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

Mineral salt medium (MSM) was prepared by mixing KH2PO4 (4.54 g), Na2HPO4⋅12H2O (11.94 g), NH4Cl (1.0 g), MgSO4⋅7H2O (0.5 g), and CaCl2⋅2H2O (5 mg) with 1 L of deionized water, pH 7.0. MSM containing 0.1% (w/v) PBS emulsion with or without 2% (w/v) agar was used as the PBS-emulsified medium for the isolation and cultivation. The PBS emulsion was prepared according to previous reports with some modifications (Teeraphatpornchai et al., 2003). PBS particles (0.2 g) were dissolved in 10 mL of dichloromethane. The solution was mixed with 100 mL of MSM and emulsified by sonication (300 W, 10 min) using 0.01% (w/v) Plysurf A210G (Daiichi Kougyou Seiyaku, Tokyo, Japan) as an emulsifier. The resulting emulsion was stirred at 70 °C for 1 h to remove dichloromethane and to form the PBS emulsion.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Investigation of morphology, enzyme-producing capacity, and degradation of polyester by P. mendocina SA-1503
ce:section.ce:para: A bacterial suspension was prepared by incubating P. mendocina SA-1503 in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium at 30 °C for 20 h. The bacterial suspension was dropped onto a coverslip coated with 1% lysine and fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 2 h. The coverslip was vigorously rinsed with saline and then treated with 2% tannic acid for 2 h. After re-washing with saline, the coverslip was dehydrated using ethanol at different concentrations (25%, 50%, 75%, and anhydrous ethanol). After air-drying, the samples were sprayed with gold before being subjected to morphological studies using a Hitachi SU8010 scanning electron microscope (SEM, Tokyo, Japan).

Pseudomonas mendocina SA-1503 was cultured in glycerol tributyrate/rhodamine B medium and skimmed milk medium at 30 °C. The formation of clear zones was used as the indicator determining whether the strains had the ability to produce esterase/lipase and protease (Wang et al., 2023b). Pseudomonas mendocina SA-1503 was also polyester emulsion media at 30 °C. The growth of colonies and the formation of clear zones were used to evaluate the degradability of polyester plastics.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Screening of potential PBS-degrading enzyme genes
ce:section.ce:para: Considering that the reported PBS-degrading enzymes belong to extracellular hydrolases (proteases and lipases) (Kaushal et al., 2021; Rosato et al., 2022a; Srisuda et al., 2021), all hydrolase genes in the genome of Pseudomonas mendocina ymp (NCBI: txid399739) were searched. Potential genes encoding PBS-degrading enzymes, as identified by signal peptides in their amino acid sequences, were obtained using signalP5.0 (https://www.novopro.cn/tools/signalp.html), and qPCR primers specific to these genes were designed (Table S1). The genes encoding potential PBS-degrading enzyme were overexpressed in P. mendocina SA-1503 grown in PBS-emulsified medium, and their identities were verified by qPCR using the ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). PBS-emulsified medium and MSM medium containing 0.2% glucose were used to culture P. mendocina SA-1503 at 30 °C for 5 d. After the collection of cultures, the total RNA was extracted using a Bacteria Total RNA Isolation Kit (Sangon, Shanghai, China), and the cDNA synthesis was performed using M-MuLV First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Sangon, Shanghai, China).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Clonal expression and purification of PBS-degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: The 3′-primer contained the BamH I digestion site and the 5′-primer contained the Xho I digestion site. The PCR primers (Table S2) were designed based on selected gene sequences (HP, TGL1, ABH1, and ABH4) and the protocols of the Ready-to-Use Seamless Cloning Kit (Sangon, Shanghai, China). The PCR conditions were as follows: 1 cycle of 5 min at 94 °C, and 30 cycles each of 45 s at 94 °C, 45 s at 50 °C, and 1 min at 72 °C. The target DNA fragments and pET-28a(+) vector linearized with BamH I and Xho I were added to a PCR tube at a molar ratio of 3:1 for the recombination reaction using the seamless cloning kit. The obtained recombinant plasmids were transformed into E. coli Arctic express (DE3) and cultured in LB medium containing 50 μg/mL kanamycin at 37 °C for 16 h. The obtained positive clones were cultured, and the gene expression was induced by IPTG to test whether the target proteins were correctly expressed. The target proteins were purified using His-tag Protein Purification Beads (BeaverBeads, Suzhou, China). The expression and molecular weight of the target protein were detected by SDS-PAGE. The protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Specific steps for inducible expression, protein purification, and SDS-PAGE are described in the Supplementary Material.

ce:section.ce:section-title: PBS degrading-enzyme activity assay
ce:section.ce:para: The PBS-degrading activity of the recombinant protein was determined following the method of Hu et al. with some modifications (Hu et al., 2016). After 250 μL of enzyme solution was added to 750 μL of PBS emulsion, the mixture was incubated at 40 °C for 20 min. The absorbance at 630 nm before and after the reaction was measured using a MultiskanGO microplate spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). One unit of PBS degrading enzyme activity is defined as the decrease in the absorbance at 630 nm by 0.001 per minute.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of temperature, pH, metal ions, and chemicals on the activity of PBS-degrading enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The optimum pH for PBS degradation of the purified enzyme was in 20 mM buffer (pH 4.0–6.0, acetate buffer; pH 6.0–8.0, phosphate buffer; pH 8.0–10.0; Tris-HCl buffer) and PBS emulsion at the same pH at 40 °C. The optimum temperature was determined by measuring the degradation capacity at different temperatures (30–65 °C) and the optimum pH. In contrast, the pH stability and thermal stability of the enzyme were determined by measuring the relative activity of the enzyme at pH 4–10 for 24 h at the optimum temperature or at 30 °C–90 °C at the optimum pH for 12 h. Several metal ions and chemicals were added to the PBS emulsion, and their effects on the PBS degrading activity of the enzyme were determined. The enzyme activity without the addition of any metal ions or chemicals was defined as 100%. Enzyme-free buffer was used as a blank control and the data from which were used to determine the change in turbidity caused by non-enzymatic factors.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity of PBS-degrading enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The p-NP esters of fatty acids with different carbon chain lengths were solubilized in isopropanol and then used to prepare 1 mM solutions in 20 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 9.0). The p-NP esters substrate was mixed with PBS-degrading enzyme solution (300 μg/mL) at a ratio of 20:1, and the absorbance at 410 nm was measured after incubating at 40 °C for 10 min and used to calculate the p-NP production (Li et al., 2020; Li and Yu, 2013). The highest p-NP yield was defined as 100%, and all other results were converted to relative percentages. The ability of PBS-degrading enzyme to hydrolyze ester bonds formed by fatty acids of different carbon chain lengths was compared. Enzyme-free buffer was used as a blank control and the data from which were used to determine the change caused by non-enzymatic factors.

After being prepared at different concentrations (0–10 mM), the p-NP ester substrates were mixed with the enzyme solution, each at a ratio of 20:1. The reaction was carried out at 40 °C for 10 min. The amount of p-NP produced was measured, and the kinetic parameters of the enzyme reaction, including K m, V max, and K cat, were calculated.

The enzyme solution (300 μg/mL) was mixed with the emulsion of PBS, PLA, PBAT, PCL, or P34HB at a 1:3 ratio and then incubated at 40 °C. The clarification of the emulsions, which indicates the polyester degradation ability of the enzyme, was observed periodically. The preparation method of polyester emulsions was similar to that of PBS.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBS films by PBS-degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para:
The PBS films (1 cm × 1 cm × 0.3 cm) were mixed with the enzyme solution (5 mL, 300 μg/mL) and incubated at 40 °C for 60 h. The film samples were removed every 12 h; after that, they were washed, dried, and weighed. The weight losses of the films were calculated according to the following equation.

The surface microstructures and hydrophilic properties of the degraded PBS films were studied by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU8010, Tokyo, Japan) and water contact angle (WCA) (Kruss DSA100, Hamburg, Germany), respectively. PLA films were cleaned, and the film surfaces were sputter-coated with gold before being subjected to SEM analysis. The WCA was measured five times under static conditions at room temperature. The degradation products of PBS were analyzed using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS, Applied Bio-systems 4700 Proteomics Analyzer, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The analysis conditions were as follows: capillary voltage, 3.5 kV; tapered hole voltage, 20 kV; RF lens voltage, 0.5 V, and source temperature, 120 °C.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Structure prediction and molecular docking of PBS-degrading enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The three-dimensional (3D) structures of the PBS-degrading enzyme were modeled using the SWISS-MODEL server (https://swissmodel.expasy.org/), and the structures presented in the figures were prepared using PyMOL2.6 software. The structures of succinic acid and 1,4 butanediol and the monomers of PBS were obtained from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). The dimer was built by the dehydrative condensation of succinic acid with 1,4 butanediol using OpenBabel 3.1.1 software (Kimura et al., 2023). The dimer unit was molecularly docked as a ligand with PBS-degrading enzymes using PyMOL 2.6 and AutoDock 4.2 software, and the interactions between the dimer substrate and enzyme molecules were predicted.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Statistical analysis
ce:section.ce:para: All experiments were performed in triplicate. The statistical analysis was carried out by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Duncan's multiple range test (DMRT) or Student's t-test using SPSS 26 software. The values were presented as mean ± SD, and the results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05 or p < 0.01.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Results and discussion
Enzyme production and degradation of polyester by P. mendocina SA-1503
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 1 shows the micro-morphologies of SA-1503 strain, and its ability to produce proteases and esterases and degrade various polyesters. According to the SEM image, SA-1503 cells appeared as slightly curved bacilli, with approximately 1.0–1.5 μm in length and 0.3–0.5 μm in width. After P. mendocina SA-1503 was cultured in glycerol tributyrate/rhodamine B medium and skimmed milk medium at 30 °C for 2 d, the colonies showed normal growth and could form clear zones. This indicates that P. mendocina SA-1503 has the ability to produce esterase and protease. PBS-degrading enzymes have been reported to belong to esterases (Kaushal et al., 2021) and proteases (Srisuda et al., 2021). The esterase and protease-producing ability of P. mendocina SA-1503 is a prerequisite for its effective PBS degradation ability. P. mendocina SA-1503 could form clear zones on PBS, P34HB, and PCL emulsion media, but not on PBAT and PLA emulsion media. This suggests that the strain has the ability to degrade PBS, P34HB, and PCL, not PBAT and PLA. The largest diameter of the clear zone generated by the strain was observed on the PBS-emulsified medium. Hence, the strain could be considered a PBS-degrading strain. Moreover, the polyester-degrading enzyme it produced could also be defined as a PBS-degrading enzyme.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Selection of PBS-degrading enzyme genes
ce:section.ce:para: Genes encoding eight potential PBA-degrading enzymes were screened from the genome of P. mendocina ymp (Table S1). RT-qPCR technique was used to verify the differences in the expression levels of these genes when the strains were cultured with PBS and glucose as the sole carbon sources. The results (Fig. 2 ) showed that triacylglycerol lipase 2 (TGL2), triacylglycerol lipase 3 (TGL3), α/β hydrolase 2 (ABH2), and α/β hydrolase 3 (ABH3) were not expressed when PBS was used the sole carbon source. On the other hand, triacylglycerol lipase 1 (TGL1), α/β hydrolase 1 (ABH1), α/β hydrolase 4 (ABH4), and a hypothetical protein (HP) showed a significant increase in expression, which suggests that these four genes are likely to be the genes encoding PBS-degrading enzymes. Therefore TGL1, ABH1, ABH4, and HP were selected for clonal expression for subsequent experiments.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression and purification of PBS-degrading enzymes
ce:section.ce:para: Four potential genes encoding PBS-degrading enzymes, including HP, TGL1, ABH1, and ABH4, were PCR-amplified and ligated to PET-28a(+). They were transformed into E. coli Arctic Express (DE3) for recombinant expression. Only HP and TGL1 could successfully express the target protein (Figs. S1 and S2). ABH1 also successfully expressed the target protein after the replacement of the PET-32a(+) vector (Fig. S3), while ABH4 did not. The molecular weights of the recombinant proteins HP, TGL1, and ABH1 were about 27.5 kDa (Fig. 3 ), 30 kDa, and 55 kDa, respectively (ABH1 contained Trx-tagged protein sequences, and its actual molecular weight was about 32.5 kDa). HP, TGL1, and ABH1 were mainly expressed in the precipitate of the recombinant cells after fragmentation as inclusion bodies (IBs), which are common for overexpression of exogenous genes in prokaryotic expression systems (Romana and Jozef, 2021). Obtaining biologically active proteins from IBs is a complex procedure that requires isolation, solubilization, refolding, and purification of IBs (Singh et al., 2015). In this study, biologically active ABH1 and TGL1 were not obtained after attempting various refolding methods. Purified HP had PBS degradation ability; hence, the enzymic properties and PBS degradation ability of only HP were studied.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of temperature, pH, metal ions, and chemicals on HP activity
ce:section.ce:para: Figs. 4 A and B shows that the optimal pH and temperature of HP were 9.0 and 40 °C, respectively. The assays for pH stability (Fig. 4C) and thermal stability (Fig. 4D) showed that HP could retain more than 40% of its activity at the temperature range of 30–50 °C for 12 h. Similarly, over 50% of its activity could be retained over a wide pH range (pH 6.0–10.0) for 24 h. This suggests that neutral and alkaline pH environments and moderate temperatures are more suitable for HP.

The enzyme activity depends on the type and concentration of metal ions in the reaction. This is due to the interactions between the metal ions with the charged amino acids of the enzyme molecule, which affect the conformation and stability of the enzyme (Noor et al., 2006). The addition of 1 mM of Mn2+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and Fe2+ significantly promoted the HP activity, whereas the addition of Cu2+, Zn2+, and Fe3+ resulted in the loss of enzyme activity by more than 70% (Fig. 4E). When the metal ion concentration reached 10 mM, only Mn2+ could promote the HP enzyme activity, which suggests that Mn2+ plays an important role in enzyme catalysis.

At a low concentration (1%), methanol, glycerol, β-mercaptoethanol, ethanol, EDTA, Triton X-100, Tween 80, and SDS inhibited HP. The inhibition of HP activity of Triton X-100, Tween 80, and SDS was significantly higher than that of other chemicals. This inhibitory effect was more pronounced when the concentration of the chemicals was higher (10%), and only methanol had a relatively minor inhibitory effect (Fig. 4F). Plou et al. demonstrated that Tween 80 acts as a competitive inhibitor and could bind to esterases and lipases (Plou et al., 1998) and inhibit their activity. However, the activity of cutinase ANCUT2 from Aspergillus nidulans can be inhibited by 5% SDS, which causes a conformational change in the enzyme (Bermúdez-García et al., 2017).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity and kinetic parameters of HP
ce:section.ce:para: The p-NP fatty acid ester substrate could be used to determine the preference of proteins with unknown functions for ester bonds formed by fatty acids of different lengths (Huo et al., 2018). Generally, esterases preferentially hydrolyze short-chain fatty acid esters (<8 carbon atoms), while lipases preferentially hydrolyze long-chain fatty acid esters (>8 carbon atoms) (Dodson et al., 1992). Purified HP could hydrolyze all the p-NP substrates with the number of carbons from C2 to C18 (Fig. 5 A); nonetheless, it had higher hydrolytic ability for short carbon chain fatty acid substrates (C2-C6), with the highest activity for C6 substrates. Therefore, HP should be considered an esterase. Previous reports suggest that esterase from Pseudomonas sp. belongs to the bacterial esterase/lipase family VIII and shows a preference for short-chain p-NP esters (Xu et al., 2015). In contrast, carboxylesterase PA 3859 from P. aeruginosa shows a preference for p-NP palmitate (C16) (Pesaresi and Lamba, 2010). The effect of substrate concentration on the rate of HP-catalyzed reaction was studied using p-NP ester at different concentrations as the substrate. Lineweaver-Burk plot (Fig. 5B) was plotted using the substrate concentration and p-NP formation rate. HP had a smaller K m and larger V max when p-NP esters C2-C8 were used as substrates (Table S3). HP had the highest affinity for p-NP C2, followed by p-NP C4 and p-NP C6. Overall, the longer the chain length of the substrate, the weaker the affinity to HP. HP had the smallest K cat for p-NP C6, which indicates that it had the highest catalytic effect on p-NP C6 substrates.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation ability of HP on different polyesters
ce:section.ce:para: The ability of HP to degrade different polyesters was investigated by determining the changes in turbidity of polyester emulsions (Fig. 6 ). HP could completely clarify the PBS emulsion within 24 h. HP also had a good hydrolysis effect on PCL and P34HB. The degradation ability of HP on PLA and PBAT was weak, and the turbidity of the emulsion did not change significantly compared to that before degradation. The degradation ability of HP in degrading different polyesters could be ranked in the following order: PBS﹥PCL﹥P34HB﹥PLA ≈ PBAT. This is consistent with the previous results, wherein P. mendocina SA-1503 formed clear zones in the polyester emulsion medium. This further indicates that HP is a multifunctional polyester-degrading enzyme. It has been previously reported that some PBS-degrading enzymes have the ability to degrade other polyesters. An extracellular lipase from Amycolatopsis mediteranei can rapidly hydrolyze PCL and PBS, but cannot hydrolyze PLA (Tan et al., 2021). An esterase from Bacillus sp. JY 35 can hydrolyze PHB, PHA, PBAT, PBS, and PCL (Kim et al., 2023). Est-H and Est-L esterases from Roseateles depolymerans TB-87 can degrade poly(butylene succinate)-co(butylene adipate) (PBSA), PCL, and poly(butylene succinate)-co-(butylene terephthalate) (PBST) (Shah et al., 2013). The differences in the degradation ability of enzymes in degrading different polyesters can be explained in terms of both substrate and enzyme. There are differences in the chemical structure of different polyester substrates, including monomer composition, chain length, crystallinity, and branched structure. These differences can affect the enzyme-substrate molecule interaction and thus the degradation efficiency (Zambrano et al., 2020). In addition, the molecular weight and degree of polymerization of the polyester can affect its chain length and molecular complexity, which in turn affects the degradation efficiency (Gu et al., 2024). The differences in the degradation efficiency of enzymes in the degradation of different polyesters are also related to the substrate specificity of the enzyme. Enzymes may have a higher affinity to ester bonds of certain polyesters, which in turn leads to higher catalytic efficiency (Rosato et al., 2022a).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBS films by HP
ce:section.ce:para: The PBS films were incubated with 300 μg/mL HP solution for 60 h (Fig. 7 ). The weight loss of PBS films gradually increased with time. The weight loss of PBS films was only 11.3% at 12 h of incubation, which was relatively low. Thereafter, as the incubation time was prolonged, the weight loss of the film continuously progressed until reaching about 60% at 48 h. As the incubation continued, the increase in weight loss was no longer significant. In the previous pre-experiment in which 100 μg/mL HP was used to treat PBS films for 48 h, the weight loss of the film was less than 10%. This indicates that the PBS degradation efficiency of HP is concentration-dependent (Lin et al., 2023).

SEM images (Fig. 8 ) show that the surface of PBS film without HP-catalyzed degradation was smooth and flat. After 12 h of degradation, the surface of the film became rough and uneven with depressions, which is due to the initial erosion of the PBS film by HP. Thereafter, cracks and holes appeared on the surface of the film, which increased and deepened as the degradation time was prolonged. The WCAs of the PBS films after HP degradation were also measured (Fig. S4). The WCA decreased with time. This indicates that the HP-catalyzed degradation reduces the hydrophobicity of PBS films. Due to the reduction in hydrophobicity, the probability of the binding of enzyme molecules to the films increased.

The analysis of PBS degradation products of HP by MALDI-TOF-MS showed several new peaks (Fig. 9 B) compared to those of the control (without HP) (Fig. 9A). The peaks at m/z 89 and 117 corresponded to monomers from PBS, 1,4-butanediol (B) and succinic acid (S), respectively. In addition, a series of oligomers consisting of less than or equal to 7 monomers were detected. It can be hypothesized that HP randomly hydrolyzes ester bonds in the PBS molecule. HP also belongs to endonucleases, which is consistent with the findings reported by Mao et al. (2015).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Prediction of the tertiary structure of HP and its molecular docking with the PBS-forming dimer
ce:section.ce:para: The amino acid sequence of HP was compared by the SWISS-MODEL and found to be 93% similar to that of Chain A of lipase (PDB: 2FX5_A) from P. mendocina. HP contained a typical folded structure, with eight essential parallel β-folds forming a central β-sheet. The center of the protein core was surrounded by five α-helices, wherein the α-helices and β-folds were connected by flexible loops (Fig. 10 A and B). This is similar to those of most esterases with microbial origins (Nardini and Dijkstra, 1999). The catalytic triad consisting of Ser-148, Asp-198, and His-228 spatially aggregated to form an active site of the core structural domain to perform its function (Hosokawa, 2008). Therefore, HP could be classified as a microbial esterase of the α/β hydrolase superfamily with a conserved catalytic triad structure. Comparison of the amino acid sequence of HP with that of other reported PBS-degrading enzymes, such as lipase from Saccharomonospora viridis (Miyakawa et al., 2015), Acidovorax delafieldii (Uchida et al., 2002), Amycolatopsis mediterranei U32, and Moraxella sp. TA144 (Feller et al., 1990), and cutinase from Thermobifida cellulosilytica (ADV92526.1) (Gamerith et al., 2017) (Fig. S5) revealed that HP shared multiple similar sequences and conserved regions with these PBS-degrading enzymes. The structural similarity of enzymes usually reflects the similarity of their catalytic mechanisms (Riziotis et al., 2022). HPs with a similar structure to the reported PBS-degrading enzymes may use a similar catalytic strategy to break the ester bonds in order to degrade polyester plastics such as PBS. This similarity is essential to understanding how degrading enzymes from different sources can function in the same way and predict how new enzymes can degrade their respective substrates.

The catalytic function of an enzyme depends on the binding and catalytic groups at its active center, as well as its spatial structure. A molecular docking technique was used to predict the binding mode of HP to the PBS substrate and generate the docking between HP and succinic acid-butanediol dimer. This binding was visualized using PyMOL2.6 software (Fig. 10C). The active center of HP was found to bind to the dimer. In addition to the catalytic triad (Ser-148, Asp-198, and His-228), amino acid residues such as His-147 and Thr-80 were found to be associated with the dimer. Thr-80 formed three hydrogen bonds with the substrate with bond lengths of 1.94 Å, 3.17 Å, and 3.22 Å, while each of His147 and Ser148 formed a hydrogen bond with the substrate with bond lengths of 2.64 Å and 2.01 Å, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Conclusion
ce:section.ce:para: In this study, an esterase (HP) with PBS-degrading ability, was obtained from P. mendocina SA-1503. HP had a relatively exposed active site with an active central catalytic triad comprising Ser-148, Asp-198, and His-228. The amino acid sequence in HP was similar to those of some lipases and cutinases, which have PBS-degrading ability. The degradation products of HP included succinic acid, 1,4-butanediol, and their oligomers. Furthermore, HP could degrade PCL and P34HB; thus, it could be categorized as a multifunctional polyester-degrading enzyme. These results help us to further understand the PBS degradation mechanism of the enzyme and provide a basis for the future development of technologies for biodegradation and recycling of aliphatic polyesters, represented by PBS. However, it is necessary to carry out rational evolution and molecular modification of the degradation enzymes to improve their thermal stability and catalytic activity to meet the requirements of large-scale applications.
